title: Sebastian and the Radiators
premise: After his mother's funeral, Felix Yarrow returns to the family house to sort her belongings and discovers she spent her final decade secretly funding a dying language, Vessic, spoken fluently by only one man: Anselm Rook, a former political prisoner his mother helped free. When Anselm asks Felix to become his last student, Felix learns that his mother's silence concealed complicity in the regime that destroyed the language—and that the stranger in the old photographs is himself, as a child, already part of the story. As Anselm's health fails, Felix must choose between cataloging the past safely or speaking it aloud at a public inquiry into the old regime's crimes. He testifies in Vessic, forgiving his mother by finally hearing her, and the book ends with him teaching the first new student in a language that was supposed to die.
about_author: Juniper Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloging oral histories from post-authoritarian communities before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, silence, and the small acts of repair that outlast institutions.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Three weeks after the funeral, Felix moves through his childhood home like a renter, labeling boxes he can't bring himself to open. The emotional beat is numb avoidance—he keeps finding evidence of a mother more complicated than the one he mourned, and keeps putting it back in the dark.

chapters.title: What the Boxes Keep
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. In a locked drawer, Felix finds bank statements showing monthly payments to someone named A. Rook for eleven years, plus photographs of his mother with strangers outside a prison wall. The beat is the first crack: curiosity displacing grief, and the unsettling sense that his mother had a life he was never admitted to.

chapters.title: A Man Who Counts His Words
chapters.summary: Felix tracks Rook to a coastal town and finds Anselm Rook, elderly and precise, who greets him by name before introductions. Anselm reveals he is the last fluent speaker of Vessic. The beat is disorientation—Felix expected a debtor or a blackmailer, and found instead a man waiting for him.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Anselm explains his offer: teach Felix Vessic before he dies, because a language needs two people or it becomes a specimen. He withholds why Felix specifically. The beat is quiet gravity; Anselm has chosen this moment for years and refuses to hurry it now.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Reluctant lessons begin. Vessic has no word for 'owner,' only 'keeper'—a distinction that unsettles Felix's whole relationship to the house and his inheritance. The beat is reluctant wonder: the language rearranges things he thought were settled.

chapters.title: The Photographs, Again
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Studying the prison photographs, Felix realizes one blurred child in the frame is himself, age seven, on a day he cannot remember. He confronts Anselm, who says only: 'You were there. Ask your questions in order.' The beat is vertigo—the past stops being background.

chapters.title: The Regime's Long Tail
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Research reveals his mother testified against collaborators after the fall—or was supposed to. Her name appears in inquiry records as a witness who withdrew. Meanwhile a government commission announces public hearings on regime crimes. The beat is rising stakes: history is reopening whether Felix likes it or not.

chapters.title: Grammar of Blame
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Lessons deepen: Vessic verbs mark whether an action was witnessed. Anselm teaches Felix to say 'I saw' and notices the boy flinch. The beat is tenderness with an edge—Anselm knows what he is asking Felix to become capable of saying.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Old Photographs
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A neighbor identifies the other adults in the photo: resisters, one of whom informed on the group. Felix's mother knew the informer—possibly loved him. The beat is betrayal compounded: the silence wasn't protection, it was shame, and Felix begins to resent being made its heir.

chapters.title: Withdrawal
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Angry, Felix stops the lessons and starts selling the house, accelerating his exit. But he translates nothing all week and finds the silence of unspoken Vessic worse than grief. The beat is self-betrayal recognized—the language has already colonized him.

chapters.title: Anselm's Hospital
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Anselm is hospitalized; his memory of recent words frays while old Vessic stays vivid. He rehearses the story he has never told anyone, in the language built for witnessing. The beat is mortality pressing the clock: the transmission cannot wait for Felix's comfort.

chapters.title: The Night Visit
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix visits the hospital at night and finds Anselm dreaming aloud in Vessic—prison interrogation transcripts surfacing verbatim. Felix understands his mother paid not out of guilt but penance: she was the informer's daughter, and she hid a child witness. Him. The beat is devastating clarity.

chapters.title: Why Me
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Recovering enough to speak, Anselm tells Felix plainly: the child in the photograph saw the informer's face, and only a living witness can corroborate the testimony the inquiry lacks. He never wanted a student; he wanted a voice. The beat is anger meeting honesty—manipulation and rescue braided together.

chapters.title: Keeper, Not Owner
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix halts the house sale and reopens every box, reading his mother's letters properly for the first time. He finds her unsent draft testimony, written in Vessic so no one could censor it. The beat is reconciliation begun at a distance—forgiving the stranger in the photographs means finishing her sentence.

chapters.title: Translation as Testimony
chapters.summary: Felix and Anselm work through the draft together, Felix translating line by line, learning the grammar of confession. Anselm corrects not the facts but the witnesses' names, restoring those history erased. The beat is shared purpose: two men building a bridge across a destroyed country, word by word.

chapters.title: Pressure
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A lawyer representing surviving regime officials contacts Felix, hinting that a withdrawn witness's son might prefer discretion—offering to buy the house and its contents. The beat is corruption arriving politely, and Felix discovering that power still wants the past kept dark.

chapters.title: The Offer Refused
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix declines and is threatened subtly—his mother's reputation, his own standing. He almost folds, then remembers there is no Vessic word for owner, only keeper. The beat is resolve hardening into identity: he decides what kind of heir he will be.

chapters.title: Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Knowing he may not last the month, Anselm gives Felix the final lesson: how to teach, not just speak. 'A language dies when it becomes private,' he says. The beat is succession—an old man handing over a flame and making peace with the burn marks.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Climax. At the public inquiry, Felix delivers his mother's testimony in Vessic, then translates it aloud, naming the informer and the witnessed crime, his voice shaking but unbroken. Officials squirm; survivors weep. The beat is justice outside the law's timetable—truth spoken in a tongue the powerful assumed was dead.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The testimony ripples: archives reopen, families contact Felix, and the officials' lawyer's threats collapse into irrelevance. Anselm, watching from home, hears his language on the radio for the first time in fifty years. The beat is exhausted, astonished relief.

chapters.title: Two Speakers
chapters.summary: Anselm's POV. Anselm dies in early autumn, lucid, with Felix reciting beside him—not mourning but conversing, in Vessic, until the end. The beat is grief transfigured into continuity: the last speaker dies, and the language does not.

chapters.title: The First Student
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Epilogue. In the house he now keeps rather than owns, Felix begins teaching Vessic to a young archive clerk, using his mother's letters as the first text. The beat is quiet hope: forgiveness completed, silence broken, and a future where the stranger in the photographs is finally known.
